pedagogy.summary: Children reflect and translate a shape on a squared grid, give the image's coordinates, and articulate that the moved shape is congruent to the original — same size and shape, only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) has changed. The pedagogical heart is that a transformation is a rule for where every point goes, not a vague 'slide it over': reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.
bestPractices: Build reflection from the point rule, not 'flip it': for each vertex, draw the line to the mirror, note it is PERPENDICULAR to the mirror, count the squares to the line, then count the same number of squares beyond it — the image vertex lands there. Assemble the image vertex by vertex.

Explicitly avoid the language 'straight across' or 'straight down' even for vertical/horizontal mirrors; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' so the idea generalises when mirror lines later slope (NCETM KS3 6.3).

Draw attention to 'sense': after a reflection the shape reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise vertex order becomes anticlockwise). This is what distinguishes a true reflection from a shape that has merely been slid across.

Establish translation as 'every point moves the same' — model it by moving ONE vertex '5 right, 2 up', then checking every other vertex followed the identical move; the shape's orientation and sense are unchanged.
Make congruence explicit and testable: trace the original onto tracing paper and lay it over the image to confirm same size and shape; name the word 'congruent'.
Keep coordinate reading disciplined — state the image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-y reversal that surfaces whenever coordinates re-enter.
keyRepresentations: Squared/coordinate grid with a vertical (then horizontal) mirror line
Perpendicular 'joining lines' from each object vertex to its image vertex, crossed at right angles by the mirror line
Tracing paper laid over object and image to demonstrate congruence
A translation vector shown as a 'staircase' arrow (e.g. 5 right then 2 up) applied identically to every vertex
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.

learn.summary: Year 5 learners reflect and translate a scalene shape on a squared/coordinate grid, state the image coordinates as (across, up), and justify that the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape, with only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) changed. The core idea is that a transformation is a precise rule for where every point goes: reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.

activities.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
feedback: If the image reads the same way round as the original (sense not reversed), it is not a reflection. It was most likely slid (or possibly turned) rather than reflected. Rebuild it one vertex at a time using the perpendicular lines so the reversal emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line'.
If the square-counts from the mirror differ between an object vertex and its image, or the image touches the mirror line, recount perpendicular to the line on each side and make the two counts equal.

If coordinates come out as (up, across) — e.g. a corner at (5,3) reported as '(3,5)' while the plotted point is correct — re-anchor 'across first, then up' and recheck one corner together against the grid.
activities.rationale: Teaching reflection from the perpendicular point-rule, and explicitly avoiding 'straight across/down' language, targets the documented misconception that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane and generalises to sloping mirror lines later. Using a scalene shape makes the reversal of sense observable; of the two transformations in this unit, only reflection reverses sense.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (writing/reading the second value before the first); teaching should reinforce reading across before up.
learnerActions: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

activities.title: Translate every point by the same vector and contrast it with reflection
feedback: If only part of the shape moves, or vertices move by different amounts, re-apply the single vector to each vertex in turn until every corner has shifted identically.
If a learner claims the translated shape has 'turned', check the vertex order against the original: a translation leaves it reading the same way round.
Prompt: 'Is your translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' — both transformations preserve size and shape.
activities.rationale: Modelling translation as 'every point moves the same' and directly contrasting it with reflection isolates the invariant (orientation/sense preserved) that separates the two transformations. The curriculum expects Year 5 pupils to translate shapes and recognise the result is congruent.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Take the original triangle and set a single translation rule, e.g. '5 squares right, 2 squares up', shown as a staircase arrow.
Apply that identical move to ONE vertex first, then check that every other vertex has to follow the exact same move.
Complete the translated shape and confirm its orientation and sense are unchanged (it reads the same way round as the original).
Place the reflected shape and the translated shape side by side and describe the felt difference: the slide keeps sense, the flip reverses it.
Report the translated image coordinates as (across, up).
activities.intendedInsight: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so orientation and sense are unchanged — the opposite of reflection, which reverses sense. Both leave the shape congruent to the original.

activities.title: Test congruence by tracing and overlaying
feedback: If a learner says the moved shape is bigger, smaller, or 'different', lay the tracing directly over the image (turning it over for a reflection) to show the exact match, then name 'congruent'.
For a reflected image the tracing must be flipped over to match — note that this flip IS the reversed sense, and the shape is still congruent.
If a learner can overlay correctly but resists the word, restate: position changed, size and shape did not — that is what congruent means.
activities.rationale: A direct physical match makes congruence testable rather than asserted, targeting the misconception that moving a shape changes it. Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat figure, which has zero thickness; the demonstration is about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical copy.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Trace the original triangle onto tracing paper (or cut out a card copy, noting that real paper/card has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal zero-thickness flat figure it represents).

Lay the tracing directly over the translated image and confirm an exact match in size and shape; for the reflected image, turn the tracing paper OVER to make it match — this flip is itself the reversed sense, and the size and shape are still identical.
Say aloud that the moved shape is congruent to the original: only its position (and, for the reflection, its sense) has changed, not its size or shape.
Answer the challenge 'Is it a new, different triangle now?' — about the mathematical shape represented — by pointing to the exact overlay match.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection and translation change where a shape is (and reflection changes which way round it reads) but never its size or shape; the technical word for this sameness is 'congruent'.

activities.title: Diagnostic performance task: reflect, translate, and justify
feedback: Watch how the image is built rather than explaining the rule first; a block-shunted image reading the same way round signals a slide-instead-of-reflect error to reteach via the perpendicular rule.

Full response: each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically, coordinates as (across, up), congruence justified by matching/tracing, and correct transfer when the mirror line or vector changes.

Partial response: carries out both transformations and may name congruence but treats each as a remembered procedure — cannot say WHY the image sits where it does or transfer to a mirror in a new position; reteach the point rule explicitly.
If coordinates are reversed, re-anchor 'across first, then up' and check one vertex together.
activities.rationale: A watch-the-build performance task discriminates genuine understanding of the point rule from imitation, because the two documented misconceptions (unreversed sense; unequal distance from the mirror) show up in how the image is constructed. Probing the perpendicular relationship and congruence surfaces reasoning rather than recall.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Given a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right, reflect the triangle in the mirror line and state the coordinates of the reflected corners as (across, up).
Back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up, and describe the move made.
Explain whether the new triangle is the same as the first and how you know, using tracing/overlay and the word congruent.

Answer probes: What is the relationship between the line joining a corner to its image and the mirror line? If the mirror moved one square further right, what would happen to the reflected triangle? If a friend slid the triangle across without turning it, is that a reflection, and how can you tell?
activities.intendedInsight: Holding the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the correct distance AND reversed in sense; merely sliding produces the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance). Watching HOW the image is assembled — perpendicular vertex by vertex, or shunted as a whole block — separates understanding from imitation, and the congruence question separates learners who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving changes it.

constraints: Use a scalene shape so the reversal of sense is visible; a symmetric shape can hide whether a learner reflected or merely slid.
Say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' rather than 'straight across/down', even for vertical or horizontal mirrors, so the rule generalises to sloping mirror lines later.
Report image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-before-y / y-before-x reversal.
When using tracing paper to check a reflection, the tracing must be turned OVER to overlay the image; the shape remains congruent and that flip is the reversed sense.

Discrete-item checks (choosing the correctly reflected image among a slid-across distractor and a not-equidistant distractor, filling in image coordinates, true/false on congruence) can diagnose the two misconceptions but, because nothing recomputes, they check rather than build the felt rule; use them alongside, not instead of, construction.

A pre-annotated worked diagram that reveals the perpendicular joining lines, the equal square-counts and the label 'congruent' can illustrate the rule but does not let a learner test their own placement, which is the core skill; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment.

A live grid where dragging a vertex or the mirror line recomputes the image (with faint perpendicular joining lines, live square-counts that turn green when the two sides match, a sense badge that flips when the reflection is correct, a settable translation arrow applied to all vertices at once, and a ghost of the original for congruence) can make the invariants concrete; these interaction and feedback examples are optional ways to expose the mechanism, not mandatory.

Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figure; use it to demonstrate congruence of the represented mathematical shape while distinguishing that shape from the physical copy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One legacy source claim (National Curriculum, Year 5 reflect/translate/congruence) was marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activities 2, 3 and 4; it directly supports the congruence principle and is the only curriculum source for it, but its evidential status is unconfirmed, so treat its citation accordingly.

The legacy entry framed a 3D rendering and an in-role dialogue as 'poor' for this planar skill. Those are catalog-fit judgements, not universal laws: a planar grid is well suited to square-counting and depth is not used here, but no claim of universal impossibility is made. These alternatives were not carried forward as activities because they do not let the learner construct and verify a reflection; their underlying affordances are noted only as scaffolds/limits.

Legacy phrasing such as 'cannot let the child TEST their own placement' and 'adds nothing' was softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the exact sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The row's evidence statement gives a '3 units right, 2 units up' translation example, whereas the diagnostic and these activities use '5 right, 2 up'; the activities follow the diagnostic consistently.

probeDeeper: Point at one object vertex and its image and ask: 'What can you tell me about the line joining these two corners and the mirror line?' (listen for perpendicular / equal distance, not 'it's across from it').
'If I moved the mirror line one square further right, what would happen to your reflected triangle?' (tests that the image is defined by distance from the mirror, not a fixed spot).
Counterexample: 'Your friend slid the triangle straight across to here without turning it round — is that a reflection? How can you tell?' (listen for sense/orientation reversal being absent).
'You translated it 5 right and 2 up. Is the translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' (congruence is preserved by both transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: The child places each reflected vertex perpendicularly opposite its original at an equal number of squares beyond the mirror line, so the image is equidistant and its sense is reversed (a scalene triangle visibly reads the other way round); reports the image coordinates as (across, up); translates by moving every vertex 5 right and 2 up together; and states the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape — checking by matching or tracing, understanding only position (and, for the reflection, orientation/sense) changed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects by sliding the whole shape across the mirror without reversing it, so its sense is unchanged ('I just moved it over to the other side')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the line from one vertex to the mirror, show it meets the mirror at a right angle, count the squares and count the same beyond; repeat per vertex so the reversed sense emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across' language.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image reads the SAME way round as the original (vertex order not reversed) — for a scalene triangle the 'point' faces the same direction; the child moves the shape as one block rather than vertex by vertex.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often letting the shape touch the line or miscounting one side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count squares perpendicular from each vertex to the line, then step the identical count to the far side; mark both counts and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Square-counts from mirror differ between object and image; image sits closer to or on the mirror line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the shape changes size or becomes a different shape once moved, so it is no longer 'the same' ('it's a new triangle now')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the original and lay it over the image to show an exact match; name 'congruent' — position (and sense) changed, size and shape did not.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the moved shape is bigger/smaller or 'different'; cannot justify sameness or resists the word congruent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the reported image coordinates, giving the up-value before the across-value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor then up the stairs': read across first, then up; check one vertex together against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a landed vertex as (up, across) — e.g. calls (5,3) '(3,5)' — while the plotted point is actually correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place a correct image: slides the shape across with unchanged sense or at an unequal distance, and treats the moved shape as changed or 'new'. Coordinates may also be reversed.
responseLevels.full: Builds both images from the point rule — each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant across the mirror with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically — reports image coordinates as (across, up), and justifies congruence by matching/tracing, transferring correctly when the mirror line or vector is changed.
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a reflection and a translation and may name congruence, but treats each as a remembered procedure — e.g. reflects correctly in a vertical mirror yet cannot say WHY the image sits where it does (perpendicular, equidistant), or reports the steps without connecting them to the shape staying congruent. Lists the moves but cannot explain how the point rule forces the image, nor transfer to a mirror in a new position.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right. Say: 'Reflect this triangle in the mirror line, then tell me the coordinates of the reflected corners. Now, back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up and describe the move you made. Last, tell me: is your new triangle the same as the first one, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how the image is built — do not explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the right distance AND reversed in sense; a child who merely 'slides it across' produces an image that is the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance), so watching HOW the image is assembled — vertex by perpendicular vertex, or shunted whole — separates real understanding from imitation. The congruence question further separates children who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving it changes it.
